design_note: Make a run-wide deadline visible as diminishing time rather than fresh per-component timeouts. The arithmetic shows why a downstream default must be clipped to the remaining allowance even though the component itself has barely started.

source.title: Deadlines
source.concept: A downstream call should honor the original deadline by accounting for time already elapsed. Cancellation also requires the server application to stop spawned work.
source.scope: Original serial ShopAssist timing uses constructed durations. It illustrates deadline propagation without claiming universal automatic propagation or hard preemption of arbitrary code.

lesson.anchor: The execution loop, end to end
lesson.title: Every boundary inherits the time already spent
lesson.intro: A read-only ShopAssist run has 20 seconds until its absolute deadline. These constructed durations show the remaining allowance before the final drafting call; each stage runs serially.

entries.label: Before final drafting: no time used

data.rule: Debit elapsed time, not reservations. The next timeout cannot exceed the remaining 6 seconds.

read: The original deadline has already lost 14 seconds to completed work.
The final adapter receives at most 6 seconds, even if its default is 30.
A new component does not create a new run deadline.
lesson.question: If the final adapter has a default timeout of 30 seconds, what maximum timeout fits this remaining run allowance?
lesson.answer: At most 6 seconds, reduced further by any time spent before dispatch. Pass the remaining deadline through the call chain and stop scheduling when it expires. The runtime still needs a supported cancellation or timeout contract; recording a deadline alone cannot preempt arbitrary work.
lesson.takeaway: Propagate remaining time instead of restarting the clock at each component.
lesson.assumption: Constructed serial timing with no clock skew; entries debit elapsed time, not spend reservations. Timeout cancellation is cooperative and does not undo effects.
